factors.what: US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5% this week, touching about 5.17% on Friday. Futures pricing shows a Fed rate hike at the Dec 9 meeting as near-certain, with a small chance of a larger half-point move. Higher US yields and a stronger dollar are the main global headwind this week.
factors.channel: A higher US rate path raises the global discount rate and tightens dollar liquidity. This can weigh on emerging-market equity valuations, rate-sensitive sectors and the rupee.

factors.what: Wall Street ended Friday lower on a chip and AI-stock pullback, but the S&P 500 still posted its best weekly gain since August. Nvidia and AMD fell sharply after Nvidia's CEO change.
factors.channel: Weakness in global tech and semiconductor stocks can spill into sentiment toward Indian IT and tech-linked names. The weekly gain shows broader global risk appetite held up.

factors.what: Brent settled near $95.8 a barrel on Friday and was down about 2.5% on the week. That followed a roughly 16% fall the week before. Supply-glut concerns and a US crude inventory build offset Middle East shipping risks. Brent is still well above its level a year ago.
factors.channel: India imports about 85% of its crude. Lower oil eases inflation and current-account pressure and helps oil marketing companies, paints, aviation and autos. It is a headwind for upstream producers.

factors.what: The US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz continues. Iran says the strait stays shut until its seven conditions are met, and Tehran rejected a US proposal on its enriched uranium stockpile. The US says it is enforcing its naval blockade. Reports of Israeli strike preparations and tanker mine incidents add to the risk.
factors.channel: The main channel is oil and LNG supply and shipping costs. Higher energy prices raise India's import bill and inflation. Escalation risk also tends to lift volatility and reduce foreign risk appetite.

factors.what: The RBI MPC raised the repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50% in October and moved to a calibrated-tightening stance. After October CPI crossed the 6% ceiling, economists broadly expect another 25 bps hike in December. SBI Research sees 25 bps rather than 50 bps, citing a steadier rupee and easier liquidity.
factors.channel: A rising policy rate lifts funding costs and bond yields. It can squeeze bank margins and weigh on rate-sensitive sectors, while a measured pace limits the tightening shock.

factors.what: On the India-US trade deal, Washington has reportedly assured New Delhi of a comparative tariff advantage over peers. The first tranche would cover goods only, and officials point to conclusion by around March. Commerce Minister Goyal said an announcement could come 'quite soon'. The deal is still unsigned and awaits clarity on the US tariff framework.
factors.channel: Clearer, lower US tariffs on Indian goods would support export-oriented sectors and reduce trade-policy uncertainty. The timing is still open.

factors.what: SEBI's new Settlement of Administrative and Civil Proceedings Regulations took effect on Nov 7. SEBI also revised underlying-exposure limits for rupee currency derivatives on Nov 5. Separately, RBI issued consolidated domestic money transfer directions and proposed limits on private-equity control of multiple NBFCs.
factors.channel: These are market-structure and regulatory changes. The currency-derivatives limits bear on rupee hedging, and the NBFC proposal bears on ownership structures in non-bank lending. They are not an immediate earnings driver.

factors.what: Retail inflation (CPI, base 2024) rose to 6.09% in October from 5.54% in September, a two-year high and above the RBI's 6% tolerance ceiling. Food inflation was 8.94%, and rural inflation (6.63%) ran above urban (5.41%).
factors.channel: Higher inflation strengthens the case for further RBI tightening and squeezes real incomes, especially in rural areas. It pressures consumption-linked sectors and rate-sensitive financials.

factors.what: India's October merchandise trade deficit widened to a one-year high of $39.88 billion, above economists' forecasts. Imports hit a record $89.35 billion on festive demand and costlier energy. Exports were also strong, with the trade secretary citing record monthly goods exports.
factors.channel: A wider deficit adds to current-account and rupee pressure, which matters for importers, oil-dependent sectors and foreign investors' currency risk. Strong exports partly offset this for exporters.

factors.what: The rupee closed at 94.24 per dollar on Friday, weaker than the previous close. A strong dollar, higher US yields and the wider trade gap are the main pressure points. SBI Research said RBI's rupee and liquidity steps and foreign fund inflows had helped stabilise conditions earlier in the month. The currency is the key channel for foreign portfolio investor appetite.
factors.channel: A weaker rupee erodes dollar returns for foreign investors and raises imported inflation. A stable rupee supports foreign participation and helps the RBI's policy path.

road_ahead.story: Oil stays near or below current levels as supply-surplus signals build and a Hormuz corridor deal gains traction. US yields ease as the Fed signals a measured hiking path. The India-US trade deal is announced with a clear tariff advantage. The RBI delivers a modest hike and signals a data-dependent pause, while rupee pressure eases.
signals: Brent holding below roughly $90 on Hormuz shipping progress
US 10-year yield falling back below 5% and Fed pricing shifting toward 25 bps
Formal announcement or signing of the India-US trade deal's first tranche
Rupee stabilising and the October WPI release (due Nov 16) coming in below expectations

road_ahead.story: Markets stay range-bound and driven by the data. US rate pricing stays hawkish into the Dec 9 Fed meeting, and oil moves on headlines without a clear break. Inflation stays above 6% near term. Markets price a 25 bps RBI hike in December, and the trade deal stays in negotiation. Solid Q2 earnings offset macro caution.
signals: Fed pricing staying near a 25 bps December hike
November CPI (due Dec 12) staying around or above 6%
RBI commentary consistent with a 25 bps move

road_ahead.story: A Hormuz or Israel-Iran escalation sends oil sharply higher, while US inflation pushes the Fed toward a half-point hike and yields climb further. Together these widen India's trade gap and weaken the rupee, and CPI stays elevated, which prompts a larger RBI hike. Trade-deal delays and renewed tariff threats add to the pressure.
signals: Brent moving back above $105-110 after tanker or infrastructure attacks
US 10-year yield rising well above 5.2% and half-point hike odds rising
Rupee breaking materially weaker than 94-95 per dollar
Food inflation staying near 9% or core inflation broadening

rules: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.

lenses.title: Through a Warren Buffett-style lens
lenses.label: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.
lenses.reason: The principles favour owning durable-moat businesses for years and discount weekly noise. Yields above 5%, 6% inflation and rate hikes raise the bar for what counts as a sensible price. The week reads as a test of pricing power and balance sheets rather than a reason to act.
watch: Whether moat businesses can pass on costs with CPI at 6.09% and food inflation near 9%
Balance-sheet strength of holdings as funding costs rise
Whether prices on quality companies offer a sensible gap to value after the rate move
avoid: Reacting to weekly swings in oil, the rupee or chip stocks
Heavily indebted businesses in a rising-rate setting
Stepping outside the circle of competence to chase a macro theme

lenses.title: Through a Charlie Munger-style lens
lenses.label: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.
lenses.reason: Inverting the problem points to what could go wrong: rising rates, an energy shock risk and a weaker rupee at the same time. The principles stress avoiding obvious mistakes before seeking gains. They also favour few decisions, so inaction is a valid response.
watch: Leverage and refinancing exposure in rate-sensitive sectors such as realty and NBFCs
Incentives behind management guidance and aggressive growth claims in a tightening cycle
Whether any quality holding is being sold or bought out of fear or excitement, not analysis
avoid: Leveraged bets on the Fed or RBI path
Businesses whose management incentives reward growth at any cost
Frequent trading around headlines on Hormuz, tariffs or chips

lenses.title: Through a Benjamin Graham-style lens
lenses.label: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.
lenses.reason: Margin of safety matters most when discount rates rise, since higher yields make bonds a stronger competitor to equities. The defensive criteria of balance-sheet strength, earnings stability and moderate valuations point to selectivity. Mr Market's daily quotes are there to be used, not followed.
watch: Whether valuations offer a wide margin of safety against 5%+ US yields
Balance-sheet strength and dividend records among candidates
Earnings stability of companies exposed to input costs and the rupee
avoid: Paying high P/E or P/B multiples on growth stories
Treating the tariff-deal headlines as settled value
Speculative positioning in oil or currency moves

lenses.title: Through a Ray Dalio-style lens
lenses.label: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.
lenses.reason: Rates, inflation and currencies are the main drivers this week: US yields above 5%, India CPI at 6.09%, a wider trade deficit and a rupee at 94.24. These are the big-move factors in his stated framework. The principles favour balancing exposures across environments rather than betting on one.
watch: The rate and dollar liquidity channel into emerging-market assets and the rupee
How oil, inflation and tightening interact across portfolio holdings
Diversification across return streams that behave differently in inflationary or tightening periods
avoid: Concentrated exposure to one rate or currency outcome
Assuming correlations hold when yields and the dollar move together
Ignoring the debt-service burden of higher rates

lenses.title: Through a Vijay Kedia-style lens
lenses.label: Not their words or views. An AI interpretation of principles they have stated publicly.
lenses.reason: The SMILE framework looks to management integrity and long-run potential in small companies, which makes the weekly macro secondary. Rate and rupee pressure matter for how well managements handle funding costs and input prices. Tariff clarity could help export-led small businesses over time.
watch: How management quality shows up in margins and balance sheets under rising rates
Small, high-aspiration companies in large markets that can compound through a tightening phase
Export-oriented businesses that could gain from tariff clarity, subject to the unsigned deal
avoid: Companies where management integrity is in doubt
Selling a sound long-term holding on short-term macro noise
Chasing themes without a large market opportunity

agree: Most lenses would stress balance-sheet strength and caution on leverage as rates rise, and would put long-term business quality ahead of weekly headlines.
disagree: Macro-focused lenses (Dalio, Marks) would treat rates, the rupee and sentiment as central, while owner-minded lenses (Buffett, Kedia, Agrawal) would look through them to business quality and management.
